title: RCMP to probe 'in-custody' death; Taser, baton used on suspect in B.C. incident: [National Edition]
subtitle: RCMP in damage-control mode
article: The death of a B.C. man following a confrontation with police in which pepper spray, a Taser stun gun and a baton were used has prompted an RCMP investigation.
Robert Thursdton Knipstrom of Chilliwack died in hospital early on Saturday, less than a week after he was injured during a struggle with police.
The RCMP is calling the incident an "in-custody death" and continues to investigate.
An analysis of the circumstances surrounding Mr. Knipstrom's death will take place alongside several similar probes ongoing across the country.

Last week the B.C. government announced a public inquiry into the Oct. 14 death of Robert Dziekanski at Vancouver International Airport. A video recording of the Polish immigrant being subdued by Taser-wielding RCMP officers provoked national debate about police use of Tasers.

The public inquiry will consider the policy governing the use of Tasers by police in B.C. At the same time, the province's Commission for Public Complaints Against the RCMP will review protocols for Taser use.
Last Thursday, Nova Scotia Justice Minister Cecil Clarke ordered a review of Taser use in the province after a 45-year-old man died in prison.

The family of Howard Hyde said he was a paranoid schizophrenic who had been arrested by Halifax Regional Police in connection with the alleged assault of his girlfriend. Mr. Hyde had been Tasered before, in 2005, his sister said.

Taser-use investigations are also being conducted in Quebec and New Brunswick. Police in Newfoundland have withdrawn a tender call for new Tasers pending the outcome of reviews in other jurisdictions.
Since 1999, at least 19 people have died after police shocked them with Tasers, according to a CBC report.

Chilliwack RCMP believe a coroner's inquest -- separate from that of the RCMP -- will shed light on the circumstances surrounding Mr. Knipstrom's death. Officers were unable to confirm that he was stunned.

"We know that the Taser was deployed in an attempt to subdue him while he was being combative with our officers, but we don't know yet if it actually made contact with him and we're hoping that the autopsy will be able to give us answers to that question," RCMP Constable Lea-Anne Dunlop said in an interview yesterday.
Reports indicate that Mr. Knipstrom, 36, had been driving erratically before entering a Chilliwack EZ Rental Centre on Monday afternoon. He became agitated when police were contacted.

Police called for backup after a struggle with Mr. Knipstrom began. Several officers were involved when he was finally restrained. In its statement on Saturday, the RCMP said it had finished the bulk of witness interviews, and that the victims of a possible hit and run had been questioned.
Mr. Knipstrom's father, Bob, apologized for his son's behaviour in a statement contained in the RCMP news release.
"The family is shocked and saddened by the recent incident between our son and the Chilliwack RCMP," he said.

"We apologize on behalf of our son to the staff of EZ Rentals for any distress that was caused because of this incident. We would appreciate that the media respect our continued privacy at this time as we grieve the loss of our son."

Mr. Knipstrom had a criminal record dating back to 1995, when he was found guilty of driving while impaired. At the time, he was given a year's probation, fined $700 and prohibited from driving for 12 months.
He was also previously charged in three other separate incidents for production of a controlled substance and possession for the purposes of trafficking, provincial court records show.
The Canada Border Services Agency also announced on Saturday that it will release its report today into the death of Mr. Dziekanski.
